coherence.reasons: Both documents run the same logical spine: launch, resize the prize from the paywall test, package in Pro with an allowance, accept the mobile delay under conditions. X maps five sub-questions to five sections, and each section's lead claim is carried by the slides beneath it. Y's four sections are tighter and equally consistent from governing thought to slide titles. Each has small blemishes. X shows the add-on break-even as 13.2% on one slide and 13.15% on another, and calls the Pro revenue gain 'near-certain' despite its own caveat on the 33% precedent. Y places the Routewise win-back under a section titled for add-on ARR, and its fourth summary point rests on a net figure that mixes a ceiling benefit with a ceiling cost. The difference in hierarchy quality is negligible.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the same defensible recommendation (R1): Pro at $12 per seat with a usage allowance, sized off the paywall test, with the mobile restart date locked. X weighs the alternatives more fully. It quantifies and rejects Copilot free in Core (71.9% margin) and a capped free tier. It compares Copilot-first against mobile-first line by line and derives a decision threshold: mobile-first wins if the rewrite prevents more than 29% of mobile churn in its first two quarters. It calls the launch-first call 'narrow' and says the deciding figure is unknown. It also notes the NRR lift is one-off and that new logos do not count in NRR. Y treats the mobile trade-off through a single net figure ($2.9M + $0.6M − $1.1M = $2.4M). That compares launching with never launching, not with launching two quarters later, so it does not really test the sequencing alternative. Y does not consider free bundling or delay as explicit options. Y's five conditions and its next steps (separate AI from the discount in win-loss data, test on non-volunteers) are good, but X's weighing of trade-offs is clearly deeper.

evidence.reasons: Both get the required calculations right: $8.06M vs $2.45M add-on ARR, inference of $32.4 / $61.2 / $130.5 per account, 109 deals and about $0.64M of win-back, and $2.89M of Pro ARR. Both debunk the sales memo (328 deals against a 109-deal ceiling), flag the Routewise discount, and treat the beta and survey as biased ceilings. Y's Pro inference cost ($1.26M plus $0.6M platform, 76% company margin) matches the key exactly. X normalises per seat (444 requests per seat, about $0.96M), a defensible but different basis. X uses more of the evidence correctly: add-on gross profit of about $0.85M, payback periods, the free-in-Core margin, the 6% AI-churn defence (about $0.48M), break-even take-up for both packages, and the small paywall sample. X's weak points are the 'near-certain' revenue gain and a somewhat mixed 29% threshold. Y's weak points are the netting slide, which adds a ceiling benefit while saying 'both risks are counted at their ceiling' and counts 33% Pro migration at face value, and a slide title that leans causal on the win-rate drop. On balance X is slightly stronger.

revision.reasons: Both handle the CPO's hypothesis as the key expects. They keep 'launch', reject the $149 add-on and the $8M survey-based sizing, resize on the 14% paywall result, explain the gap between stated and revealed demand (6% response rate, larger respondents), and show that buyers are heavy users whose inference cost erodes the flat fee. Both also reject the VP Sales claim on the same grounds. X adds a waterfall from $8M to under $1M of gross profit. Y adds an explicit planning rule ('size on what accounts paid, not what admins said'). The handling is essentially equivalent.

overall.reasons: The two documents give the same recommendation and largely the same core numbers, so the difference lies in how well each equips the CEO for the contested part of the decision: sequencing against the mobile rewrite, and packaging alternatives. X compares Copilot-first with mobile-first directly, states what would flip the answer, quantifies why free bundling fails the margin floor, gives payback and break-even headroom, and supplies a risk register and scorecard with thresholds. Y is tighter and has two good forward-looking tests (isolating the discount effect, a non-volunteer productivity test) and a useful caveat that the 2023 tier had no AI. But its treatment of the mobile trade-off is a single net figure against a no-launch baseline, and it considers fewer alternatives. X's extra length carries real reasoning, so X would serve the decision maker better.
